description: 300 mid-level logical questions on Python file handling (modes, read/write, bytes, encoding, json/csv, os/pathlib, exceptions)

questions.question: A text file poem.txt contains exactly the two lines 'twinkle twinkle' and 'little star' (that is, the content 'twinkle twinkle\nlittle star'). This code runs: `f = open('poem.txt', 'r'); print(repr(f.read())); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is `'twinkle twinkle
little star'`. read() with no argument reads the entire file from the current cursor position all the way to EOF and returns it as a single string, preserving every internal newline. The trailing newline translation in text mode has already normalized any 
 endings, so the string shows plain 
.

questions.question: poem.txt contains 'twinkle twinkle\nlittle star'. This code runs: `f = open('poem.txt', 'r'); print(repr(f.read(7))); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `'twinkle'`. read(7) reads at most the next 7 characters from the current cursor position and stops — it never reads past the 7-character limit. In text mode the argument counts characters (code points), not bytes.

questions.question: poem.txt contains 'twinkle twinkle\nlittle star'. This code runs: `f = open('poem.txt', 'r'); f.read(); print(repr(f.read())); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `''`. The first read() consumed the whole file, so the cursor is already at EOF. A second read() has nothing left to return and yields the empty string — it does not raise an error and does not rewind. The empty string is the standard 'nothing more' signal.

questions.question: numbers.txt contains 'one\ntwo\nthree'. This code runs: `f = open('numbers.txt', 'r'); a = f.readline(); b = f.readline(); print(repr(a), repr(b)); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is `'one
' 'two
'`. readline() reads from the cursor through the next newline inclusive, so the returned line keeps its trailing '
' character. Nothing is stripped automatically — you have to call strip() yourself if you do not want the newline.

questions.question: names.txt contains the characters: a l i c e newline b o b (no trailing newline at the end of the file). This code runs: `f = open('names.txt', 'r'); print(f.readlines()); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `['alice\n', 'bob']`. readlines() consumes the rest of the file and returns one list element per line, split at '\n'. Each line keeps its own trailing newline if it had one, and the final line 'bob' has none because the file does not end with a newline.

questions.question: You must process a 2 GB log file one line at a time. Compare these two approaches: `for line in f:` versus `for line in f.readlines():`. Which is memory-friendly and why?
questions.answer: Using `for line in f:` is memory-friendly. A text file object is its own iterator, so each loop iteration calls readline() internally and only the current line is held in memory at any moment. readlines() instead reads the entire file and builds one list containing every line, so all 2 GB (plus list overhead) would be in RAM at once. Iterate the file object directly for large files; readlines() suits small ones.

questions.question:
data.txt contains 'a
b
c
'. This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'r'); [print(i, repr(line)) for i, line in enumerate(f)]`. Wait, that comprehension abuses a side effect — the equivalent loop is: `for i, line in enumerate(f): print(i, repr(line))`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is:
0 'a\n'
1 'b\n'
2 'c\n'
Iterating a file object reads one line at a time until readline() returns '' at EOF. Every yielded line keeps its trailing '\n', and here the last line also has it because the file ends with a newline character.

questions.question: hello.txt contains 'hello\nworld\n'. This code runs: `f = open('hello.txt', 'r'); f.readline(); print(f.tell()); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `6`. After readline() the cursor sits just past the newline, i.e. directly after the 6 characters 'hello\n'. tell() reports the byte offset at which the next read or readline will begin; every character is 1 byte here because the content is ASCII.

questions.question: hello.txt contains 'hello\nworld\n'. This code runs: `f = open('hello.txt', 'r'); f.read(); print(f.tell()); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `12`. read() consumed the whole file and stopped at EOF, and tell() therefore equals the file size: 'hello\nworld\n' is 5+1+5+1 = 12 bytes. tell() at EOF is the reliable way to learn the byte length of the content you just read.

questions.question: hello.txt contains 'hello\nworld\n'. This code runs: `f = open('hello.txt', 'r'); f.read(); f.seek(0); print(repr(f.read())); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `'hello\nworld\n'`. seek(0) moves the cursor back to the start of the file, so the second read() re-reads the whole content. In text mode, only seek(0) and seek() to positions previously returned by tell() are guaranteed to behave sensibly.

questions.question: a file mini.txt contains 'x\ny' (it does NOT end with a newline). This code runs: `f = open('mini.txt', 'r'); print(repr(f.readline())); print(repr(f.readline())); print(repr(f.readline())); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is:
'x\n'
'y'
''
The first readline() returns the line including its newline. The second returns 'y', the last chunk of the file, with no trailing newline because the file ends there. The third call is at EOF, so it returns '' — that empty string is the standard check for end of file when using readline() in a while loop.

questions.question: data.txt contains 'hello' (5 characters, no newline). This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'r'); f.seek(3); print(repr(f.read(100))); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `'lo'`. read(100) is capped by what remains before EOF: only 2 characters are left after the cursor moves to offset 3, so it returns just those two. read() never pads, never raises, and never reads beyond EOF — it simply returns whatever is available.

questions.question: blank.txt is a completely empty file (0 bytes). This code runs: `f = open('blank.txt', 'r'); print(repr(f.read())); print(repr(f.readline())); print(f.readlines()); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is:
''
''
[]
An empty file has no data at all, so read() and readline() both give '' and readlines() gives an empty list. None of them raise an exception; you detect the absence of content by checking the empty string or empty list.

questions.question: missing.txt does not exist. This code runs: `f = open('missing.txt', 'r')`. Which exception is raised?
questions.answer: `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'missing.txt'`. Reading requires a file to read from, and 'r' (like 'r+') never creates a file, so the failure happens at open time. FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, raised before any read call is made.

questions.question: data.txt already exists. This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'x')`. Which exception is raised?
questions.answer: `FileExistsError: [Errno 17] File exists: 'data.txt'`. Mode 'x' is exclusive creation: open() creates the file for writing only if it is absent, so colliding with an existing file is reported instead of silently overwriting it. On a brand-new path, 'x' creates the file and opens it with the cursor at position 0.

questions.question: journal.txt does not exist. This code runs: `f = open('journal.txt', 'r+')`. Which exception is raised, and how does 'w+' differ in behavior for the same missing file?
questions.answer: `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'journal.txt'`. Mode 'r+' opens for both reading and writing but requires the file to already exist and never truncates. 'w+' would succeed, both reads and writes while creating the missing file — but it also truncates any existing file to zero bytes, which is the key risk of choosing it over 'r+'.

questions.question: log.txt currently contains 'old log'. This code runs: `f = open('log.txt', 'w'); f.write('new'); f.close()`. After it finishes, what exactly is inside log.txt?
questions.answer: The file contains the 3 bytes `new` — the old 'old log' content is completely gone. Mode 'w' opens for writing and truncates the existing file to zero length at open time, before any write happens. The new write then starts at offset 0, so what you write is all the file holds.

questions.question: data.txt currently contains 'AAAA'. This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'a'); f.write('BB'); f.close()`. After it finishes, what exactly is inside data.txt?
questions.answer: The file contains the 6 characters `'AAAABB'`. Append mode 'a' never truncates existing content; it positions the cursor at the end of the file on open, so every write lands after the existing bytes. The file grows from 4 bytes to 6 bytes.

questions.question: data.txt currently contains 'AAAA'. This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'a'); f.seek(0); f.write('ZZ'); f.close()`. After it finishes, what exactly is inside data.txt?
questions.answer: The file contains `'AAAAZZ'`. seek(0) moves the cursor to the start, but every write in append mode still lands at the very end of the file, because the descriptor was opened with O_APPEND and the OS forces each write to sink before it. You cannot overwrite earlier content through an 'a' handle; use 'r+' for that.

questions.question: data.bin is a binary file whose first two bytes are 0x01 0x02. This code runs: `f = open('data.bin', 'ab'); f.write(b'\x03\x04'); f.read()`. What happens?
questions.answer: The read() call raises `io.UnsupportedOperation: not readable`. Mode 'ab' is binary append: it is write-only by design, so no reading is possible at all. Because the operation is unsupported on this stream, Python raises UnsupportedOperation immediately rather than returning any data.

questions.question: f.txt currently contains 'hello'. This code runs: `f = open('f.txt', 'w+'); print(f.tell()); print(repr(f.read())); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is:
0
''
Mode 'w+' opens for both reading and writing but truncates the existing content to zero bytes immediately on open. The cursor starts at 0 and read() right away finds nothing, so you get ''. With 'w+' you must write first (then seek back) before you can read any meaningful data back.

questions.question: letters.txt contains the text 'hello'. This code runs: `with open('letters.txt', 'rb') as f: print(repr(f.read(3))); print(f.tell())`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is:
b'hel'
3
Binary mode 'rb' returns raw bytes, so read(3) produces a three-byte bytes object b'hel'. The '3' counts bytes here (in text mode it counts characters); the two numbers agree only because the content is ASCII.

questions.question: f.txt currently contains 'abcdefghij'. This code runs: `with open('f.txt', 'r+') as f: f.seek(3); f.write('XY')`. After it finishes, what exactly is inside f.txt?
questions.answer: The file contains `'abcXYfghij'`. Mode 'r+' keeps the existing bytes and write() overwrites in place at the cursor, so positions 3 and 4 become 'XY' and the characters after them ('fghij') are untouched — nothing is inserted and nothing is shifted. This in-place overwriting is the normal purpose of 'r+'.

questions.question: Match modes to behavior: for each of 'r', 'w', 'a', 'x', 'r+', 'w+', 'a+' say which (a) require the file to exist, (b) create the file if missing, (c) truncate existing content, (d) allow reading as well as writing.
questions.answer: 'r' and 'r+' require the file to exist (FileNotFoundError otherwise), never create, never truncate, and only 'r+' allows writing. 'w', 'w+', 'a', 'a+', and 'x' all create a missing file. 'w' and 'w+' truncate existing content to zero; 'a', 'a+', 'r', 'r+', 'x' do not. 'r+', 'w+', and 'a+' are the read-write modes; 'r'/'w'/'a'/'x' are single-purpose (x also writes). Also note 'w' truncates without requesting read, and 'a' writes only at the end.

questions.question: f.bin is a 5-byte file containing b'abcde'. This code runs: `with open('f.bin', 'rb') as f: f.seek(0, 2); print(f.tell())`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `5`. seek(0, 2) uses whence=SEEK_END: offset 0 positions the cursor at the end of the file, and tell() consequently equals the file size. This seek-to-end idiom is how you discover a file's length or where an append write would begin.

questions.question: f.bin is a 10-byte file containing the ASCII bytes b'0123456789'. This code runs: `with open('f.bin', 'rb') as f: f.seek(3, 0); print(repr(f.read(3)))`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `b'345'`. whence=0 (SEEK_SET) makes the offset absolute from the start of the file, so the cursor moves to byte 3, i.e. the character '3'. Reading the next 3 bytes then yields b'345'. whence=0 is the default when you call seek() with a single argument.

questions.question: f.bin is a 10-byte file containing b'0123456789'. This code runs: `with open('f.bin', 'rb') as f: f.seek(-2, 2); print(f.tell())`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `8`. whence=2 (SEEK_END) anchors the offset to the end of the file, and a negative offset moves BACKWARD from it, so the cursor lands at 10 - 2 = 8. Combining offset and whence lets you position relative to the start, the current position, or the end without knowing the exact file size.

questions.question: f.txt contains 'abc' (3 bytes). This code runs: `with open('f.txt', 'rb') as f: f.seek(100); print(repr(f.read())); print(f.tell())`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is:
b''
100
The kernel lets you seek past the end of a file without error; it simply records the huge offset 100. read() then finds nothing between the cursor and EOF and returns b'', yet the cursor stays at 100, which tell() reports. No bytes were read — the cursor simply jumped past everything.

questions.question: data.txt exists and contains 'hello world'. This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'r'); print(f.tell()); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `0`. A freshly opened file (in 'r', 'r+', 'w', 'w+', or 'x' mode) always begins with its cursor at offset 0, ready to read or write from the start. tell() reports the position of the next byte; only 'a' and 'a+' start the cursor somewhere else (at the end).

questions.question: f.bin is a large file. This code runs: `with open('f.bin', 'rb') as f: print(f.seek(10))`. What is printed, and why?
questions.answer: The output is `10`. seek() is not just a mutator: it returns the new absolute byte offset from the start of the file. That return value is handy for confirming where a relative or end-anchored move actually landed, and it equals 10 here because the offset is already absolute.

questions.question: f.txt is a new empty text file. This code runs: `f = open('f.txt', 'w'); print(f.write('hello')); f.close()`. What is printed, and what does the row '5' mean?
questions.answer: The output is `5`. In text mode write() returns the number of CHARACTERS written (in binary mode it returns bytes written). For a regular file the write is almost always complete, so the return equals the length of the string — it effectively confirms how much of the buffer made it out.

questions.question: out.txt is new. This code runs: `f = open('out.txt', 'w'); f.writelines(['line1\n', 'line2\n', 'line3']); f.close()`. What exactly is inside out.txt?
questions.answer:
The file contains `'line1
line2
line3'`. writelines() writes each string in the iterable exactly as given and adds NO newlines or separators of its own. The '
' characters are inside the string literals themselves, and because the last element 'line3' has no newline, the file does not end with one.

questions.question: f.txt is new. This code runs: `f = open('f.txt', 'w'); f.writelines([1, 2, 3])`. What happens?
questions.answer: `TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int` is raised. writelines() is just a loop that calls write() once per element, and write() requires a str in text mode (or bytes in binary mode). Integer elements are not converted, so the very first element triggers the TypeError.

questions.question: out.txt is new. This code runs: `with open('out.txt', 'w') as f: print('hello', file=f); print('world', file=f)`. What exactly is inside out.txt?
questions.answer:
The file contains `'hello
world
'`. print(..., file=f) formats exactly like print to stdout: arguments joined by spaces (never here) and followed by its default end='
' separator. So two print calls produce two lines, each terminated by a newline.

questions.question: f.txt is new. This code runs: `f = open('f.txt', 'w'); f.write(123)`. What happens, and how would you fix it?
questions.answer: `TypeError: write() argument must be str, not int` is raised. write() performs no implicit conversions: text mode accepts only str, binary mode only bytes. The fix is to convert the value yourself first, such as `f.write(str(123))` or `str(123).encode()` for a binary handle.

questions.question: f.txt is a new empty file. This code runs: `f = open('f.txt', 'w'); f.write('ab'); print(f.tell()); f.close()`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `2`. Writing advances the cursor by the number of characters written, so after 'ab' the cursor is at offset 2. tell() after a write shows exactly where the next read or write will occur — here, at the end of what you just wrote.

questions.question: f.txt is new. This code runs: `with open('f.txt', 'w+') as f: f.write('hello'); print(repr(f.read()))`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `''`. After write('hello') the cursor sits at offset 5, which is EOF for this file, and read() continues from the cursor rather than rewinding. The text you wrote is behind the cursor, so read() finds nothing — you must call f.seek(0) (or re-open the file) before you can read back what you wrote.

questions.question: f.txt currently contains 'abcdefghij'. This code runs: `with open('f.txt', 'r+') as f: f.seek(12); f.write('XY')`. After it finishes, what exactly is inside f.txt?
questions.answer: The file contains `'abcdefghij\x00\x00XY'`. seek(12) lands two bytes past the current EOF, and writing there forces a gap; regular files fill that gap with two null bytes \x00. So 'r+' lets you extend a file into sparse territory, but unless you intentionally want that, you should seek to a position at or before the file size before writing.

questions.question: f.txt exists. This code runs: `with open('f.txt', 'r') as f: content = f.read()`. Then `print(f.closed)`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `True`. The with statement runs f.__exit__() when the block ends, which closes the file automatically even though no close() was ever called. f.closed therefore becomes True the instant the block finishes — that guarantee is the entire point of the context manager.

questions.question: f.txt exists. This code runs: `with open('f.txt', 'r') as f: data = f.read()`. Then this line runs: `print(f.read())`. What happens?
questions.answer: `ValueError: I/O operation on closed file.` is raised. The variable f still refers to the handle, but the file was closed when the with block ended. Any I/O method (read, readline, write, seek, flush) called on a closed handle raises ValueError, because the underlying file system resource is no longer available.

questions.question:
f.txt exists. This code runs: `try: with open('f.txt', 'r') as f: raise ZeroDivisionError
except ZeroDivisionError: print(f.closed)`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `True`. Even when an exception jumps out of the with block, __exit__ still runs first and closes the file before the exception propagates. Closing on normal exit AND on exception is the core cleanliness guarantee of with — the file never leaks open regardless of how the block ends.

questions.question:
Fill in the single missing keyword so this snippet always closes the file whether read() succeeds or raises:
`f = open('f.txt', 'r')
try:
    data = f.read()
______:
    f.close()`
questions.answer:
The blank must be `finally`:
`f = open('f.txt', 'r')
try:
    data = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()`
finally-statement code runs in both the success and the exception path, guaranteeing the handle is released. The `with open(...) as f:` statement is the idiomatic one-liner that compiles down to exactly this try/finally semantics.

questions.question: f.txt exists. This code runs: `f = open('f.txt', 'r'); f.close(); f.close(); print(f.closed)`. What is printed?
questions.answer: The output is `True`, and no exception occurs. close() is idempotent: calling it a second time on an already-closed file is permitted and does nothing. Only other operations (read, write, seek, and friends) raise the ValueError on a closed file — double close() itself is harmless.

questions.question: On a Linux system, this code runs: `with open('/tmp', 'r') as f: f.read()`. What happens, and at which call does the failure occur?
questions.answer: `IsADirectoryError: [Errno 21] Is a directory: '/tmp'` is raised at the open() call, before f.read() is even reached. A directory is not a regular file and cannot be read as a text stream, so the OS rejects it at open time. IsADirectoryError is a subclass of OSError.

questions.question: On a Linux system, this code runs: `with open('/proc/version', 'w') as f: f.write('x')`. What happens, and at which call does the failure occur?
questions.answer: `PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/proc/version'` is raised at the open() call. The /proc pseudo-filesystem exposes read-only kernel information, so the OS refuses write access with EPERM regardless of user privileges. PermissionError, another OSError subclass, is the Python view of that refusal.

questions.question: This code runs: `with open('data.bin', 'wb') as f: f.write(b'\xff\xfe\x41')`. Then this runs: `with open('data.bin', 'r', encoding='ascii') as f: f.read()`. What happens?
questions.answer: `UnicodeDecodeError: 'ascii' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0: ordinal not in range(128)` is raised during the read() call. Text mode decodes bytes with the given codec as data flows in, and 0xff and 0xfe are not valid ASCII. Decoding happens lazily, so the error surfaces on read(), not at open() — the same file read with a UTF-8 or binary handle would succeed.

questions.question: This code runs: `f = open('data.txt', 'r', encoding='klingon')`. What happens?
questions.answer: `LookupError: unknown encoding: klingon` is raised at the open() call. The name 'klingon' is not registered in Python's codec registry, and open() looks up the encoding when the file is created. This is a codec-name lookup failure (LookupError), entirely separate from a UnicodeDecodeError, which concerns the data inside the file.

questions.question: On Linux, a file crlf.txt was transferred from Windows and contains these exact bytes: l i n e 1 \r \n l i n e 2 \r \n l i n e 3 (that is, LF lines that also carry a preceding CR). This code runs: `with open('crlf.txt', 'r') as f: print(repr(f.read()))`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is `'line1
line2
line3'`. Default text mode enables universal newline translation: 
 (and lone ) are all converted to a single '
' as the data is read. Cross-platform code therefore sees one consistent newline representation no matter which line-ending style produced the file.

questions.question: The same crlf.txt as above (bytes 'line1\r\nline2\r\nline3') is now read like this: `with open('crlf.txt', 'r', newline='') as f: print(repr(f.read()))`. What is printed?
questions.answer:
The output is `'line1
line2
line3'`. Passing newline='' disables universal newline translation, so the raw '
' byte pairs are passed through untouched. With this setting, readlines() also splits only on '
' and keeps the '' inside each returned line, which is how a parser that must distinguish '' from '
' inspects raw text.

questions.question: On Linux, a file line1.txt contains the bytes l i n e 1 \r \n l i n e 2 (one CRLF-terminated line, one bare line). This code runs: `with open('line1.txt', 'r') as f: print(repr(f.readline().strip()))`. What is printed, and what trap does strip() hide for whitespace-tolerant data?
questions.answer:
The output is `'line1'`. Universal newline translation already turned the '
' into '
' before readline(), so the first line is 'line1
', and strip() removes that trailing whitespace newline. The trap: strip() strips ALL leading and trailing whitespace (spaces, tabs, etc.), not just the newline — if the data must keep surrounding spaces, use rstrip('
') instead so only the line ending is removed.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('old data')
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('new')
print(open('data.txt').read())
```
questions.answer:
new
The 'w' mode truncates the file to zero length on open, so the first write of 'old data' is destroyed when the second open with 'w' occurs. Only 'new' remains in the file.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('start')
with open('data.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write(' end')
print(open('data.txt').read())
```
questions.answer:
start end
The 'a' mode opens the file for appending; the cursor is placed at the end of existing content, so ' end' is added after 'start' without overwriting.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'x') as f:
    f.write('created')
try:
    with open('data.txt', 'x') as f:
        f.write('again')
except FileExistsError as e:
    print(e)
```
questions.answer:
[Errno 17] File exists: 'data.txt'
The 'x' mode creates a new file exclusively. Since the file already exists from the first open, the second open raises FileExistsError.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('hello')
with open('data.txt', 'r+') as f:
    data = f.read()
    f.write('WORLD')
    print(data, f.tell())
print(open('data.txt').read())
```
questions.answer:
hello 10
helloWORLD
In 'r+' mode the cursor starts at position 0, so f.read() returns 'hello' and moves the cursor to 5. f.write('WORLD') writes 5 characters at position 5 (the end), moving the cursor to 10, so f.tell() reports 10. The file content becomes 'helloWORLD'.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('old content')
with open('data.txt', 'w+') as f:
    print(repr(f.read()))
    f.write('new')
print(open('data.txt').read())
```
questions.answer:
''
new
'w+' truncates the file to zero length, so f.read() returns an empty string. Then f.write('new') writes to the file, resulting in just 'new'.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write('data')
with open('data.txt', 'a+') as f:
    print(repr(f.read()), f.tell())
    f.write('more')
print(open('data.txt').read())
```
questions.answer:
'more' 4
datamore
In 'a+' mode the cursor starts at the end (position 4), so f.read() reads nothing. f.tell() returns 4. f.write('more') appends to the file, producing 'datamore'.

questions.question:
What is the output?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    result = f.write('hello')
    print(result)
```
questions.answer:
5
f.write() returns the number of characters (in text mode) or bytes (in binary mode) that were written. Writing 'hello' produces 5.

questions.question:
What exception is raised and why?
```python
with open('data.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(b'hello')
```
questions.answer:
TypeError: write() argument must be str, not bytes
When a file is opened in text mode (no 'b' in the mode string), f.write() expects a str. Passing bytes to a text-mode file raises TypeError.

questions.question:
What is the output?

questions.question: A file text.txt was created from the ASCII string 'hello'. What is the exact type and value of d after: d = open('text.txt', 'rb').read()?
questions.answer: <class 'bytes'> b'hello'. open with 'rb' opens in binary mode, so read() returns a bytes object, not a str. Because every byte happens to be ASCII, the repr looks like a string, but type(d) is bytes, and bytes and str are different types that never compare equal.

questions.question: What exception, with what exact message, is raised by: with open('out.bin', 'wb') as f: f.write('hi')
questions.answer: TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'. A binary-mode file object only accepts bytes-like objects (bytes, bytearray, memoryview) in write(). To write text you must encode it to bytes yourself or use a text-mode ('w') file object, which encodes using an encoding such as utf-8.

questions.question: A file words.txt contains the bytes b'l1\nl2\n'. What is printed by: print([line for line in open('words.txt', 'rb')])
questions.answer:
[b'l1
', b'l2
']. Iterating a binary-mode file yields bytes lines split at the 
 boundaries. The repr shows the bytes type prefix b and the literal 
 at the end of each line, exactly as read from disk.

questions.question: f.txt contains the 5 bytes b'hello'. Both reads are the same file: what does open('f.txt', 'rb').read() == open('f.txt').read() print?
questions.answer: False. The binary read returns b'hello' (bytes) while the text read returns 'hello' (str). Python never compares a bytes object and a str as equal, even when they contain the same characters, because equality requires the same type.

questions.question: A file t.txt was written in text mode with the string 'hi'. What is printed by: print(open('t.txt', 'rb').read())
questions.answer: b'hi'. Opening a text-created file in binary mode returns the raw bytes that were stored on disk. Binary mode performs no decoding, so you get a bytes object instead of the str that plain text reading would return.

questions.question: b.dat contains the three bytes b'\x00\x01\xff'. Running open('b.dat', encoding='utf-8').read() raises which exception, with what exact message?
questions.answer: UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 2: invalid start byte. The bytes 0x00 and 0x01 are valid UTF-8 control characters, but 0xff can never begin a valid UTF-8 sequence, so the decoder fails on it. Text mode fails loudly instead of silently producing corrupted strings.

questions.question: e.txt is written in text mode with f.write('café') using encoding='utf-8'. What does open('e.txt', 'rb').read() print?
questions.answer: b'caf\xc3\xa9'. UTF-8 encodes the character 'é' as the two bytes 0xC3 and 0xA9, so the file is 5 bytes on disk rather than 4 characters. Reading in binary mode shows those raw bytes instead of the decoded Unicode string.

questions.question: What is printed by: with open('f.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f: print(f.encoding)
questions.answer: utf-8. A text-mode file object exposes the codec it is using as the .encoding attribute, taken from the encoding= argument (or the platform default when none is given). The repr shows 'utf-8' when the string is printed.

questions.question: A file c.txt contains the UTF-8 bytes b'caf\xc3\xa9'. Running open('c.txt', encoding='ascii').read() raises which exception, with what exact message?
questions.answer: UnicodeDecodeError: 'ascii' codec can't decode byte 0xc3 in position 3: ordinal not in range(128). The ASCII codec can only map bytes in 0..127, and the byte 0xC3 (position 3 of 'café') is outside that range. Picking a codec that cannot represent the stored bytes makes text-mode decoding raise UnicodeDecodeError.

questions.question: Which exception, with what exact message, is raised by: with open('o.txt', 'w', encoding='ascii') as f: f.write('café')
questions.answer: UnicodeEncodeError: 'ascii' codec can't encode character '\xe9' in position 3: ordinal not in range(128). On write, each character is encoded with the given codec, and 'é' (U+00E9) has no ASCII mapping. This is the encode-direction counterpart of the UnicodeDecodeError raised when reading with a codec that cannot decode the bytes.

questions.question: A file is opened with open('o.txt', 'w', encoding='ascii', errors='replace') and then 'café' is written. What bytes land on disk?
questions.answer: b'caf?'. The errors='replace' error handler substitutes '?' for any character that cannot be encoded instead of raising UnicodeEncodeError. It is a pragmatic escape hatch, but it silently corrupts data, so it is usually reserved for logs or throwaway output.

questions.question: What is printed by: import sys; print(sys.getdefaultencoding())
questions.answer: utf-8. The str.encode() and bytes.decode() defaults come from sys.getdefaultencoding(), which is fixed at 'utf-8' in modern CPython. Note that open() without encoding= instead consults the locale's preferred encoding, which is also UTF-8 on this system but can differ on other machines — which is why explicit encoding= is recommended.
